extracted.intended_audience: general public; researchers, journalists and observers of press freedom and human rights in Belarus
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of laws, administrative mechanisms, technical controls, incidents, and practices that constitute censorship and media repression in Belarus. The page documents legal provisions, state institutions, tactics (legal, administrative, technical) and notable examples affecting journalists, media outlets, online platforms, and cultural producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional prohibition vs statutory enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship is formally prohibited by the country's constitution, yet it is enforced through a number of laws and administrative measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly contrasts the constitutional prohibition with the reality that various statutes, decrees and administrative practices effectively enable censorship in Belarus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law criminalizing 'insulting the president'
rubrics_metrics.description: A law making insulting the president punishable by up to five years in prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to deter and punish criticism of the head of state; cited as a statutory tool for silencing dissent and journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law criminalizing criticism of Belarus abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: A law that makes criticizing Belarus abroad punishable by up to two years in prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies extraterritorially to expressions about Belarus; used to target journalists, bloggers, or activists cooperating with foreign media or platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration/licensing requirement for all media (including websites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2009 all media outlets, including websites, need to register or face blockage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing and registration procedures are described as opaque and politicized; independent outlets have used foreign domains to avoid domestic registration. Failure to register can lead to blocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative blocking without court order after two warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Since December 2014, websites can be blocked without a court order after two warnings within 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This administrative mechanism short-circuits judicial oversight; the law also broadened 'mass media' status and extended liability to include user comments, increasing exposure to administrative sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded liability to include user comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass media status and liability were widened to include user comments on websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site owners and platforms can be held responsible for users' content, increasing legal risk and encouraging pre-moderation or deletion (self-censorship).

rubrics_metrics.name: State commission for 'extremist' material evaluation (2007 counter-extremism law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state commission established (August 2014) to evaluate whether media outlets contain 'extremist' materials, enabling bans under the 2007 counter-extremism law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The label 'extremist' carries legal consequences including bans and asset/registration actions; the commission is an administrative gatekeeper used against independent outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation requirement and prosecution of freelance/foreign journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Freelance and foreign journalists have been fined, prosecuted or expelled for working without official state accreditation; Article 22.9(2) used to fine journalists working with foreign media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fines (€200–500) and seizures of equipment were reported; procedural guarantees in prosecutions were often not observed and appeals rejected. Accreditation regimes restrict collaboration with foreign outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: State monopoly and control over broadcast media
rubrics_metrics.description: The state maintains a virtual monopoly on domestic broadcast media; only state media broadcast nationwide and content of smaller stations is tightly restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural control limits alternative viewpoints on TV/radio; independent broadcasters often cannot reach national audiences and face content restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-controlled distribution networks (printing, postal, kiosk) used to restrict circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: State-owned printing houses, post service and kiosk networks can refuse to print, distribute, or sell independent newspapers, effectively blocking circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: newspapers forced to print abroad; Belsoyuzpechat' refusing to take printed copies; postal delays and refusals used as distribution choke points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anti-extremism/defamation/obstruction laws to target journalists and outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation on extremism, defamation, obstruction of journalistic activity (e.g., Criminal Code article 198), and 'discreditation' (article 369-1) have been applied to journalists, editors, and online content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criminal/legal provisions have resulted in arrests, criminal charges, prison sentences, and labeling of content or outlets as 'extremist' to justify bans and prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative warnings and the 'two warnings' closure mechanism encouraging self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving two warnings in a year can lead to closure of a media outlet; the Ministry of Information issued many warnings (34 outlets warned in 2015 cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent warnings and the threat of closure combined with heavy defamation fines prompt outlets to self-censor to avoid sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decree #60 – registration, blacklists and other restrictive internet measures
rubrics_metrics.description: President's decree #60 (2010) provides for registration of internet resources, creation of blacklists of websites to be blocked, and other restrictive measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not all measures were necessarily used in full, the decree increased caution among internet media and encouraged softening of government criticism online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/administrative requirements on commercial websites and ISPs (2012 law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2012 law requires all commercial websites selling goods or services to Belarusian citizens to be operated from within the country under a .by domain; those who provide internet access must register all users and censor websites on a blacklist (pornography and extremist sites among them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures localize commercial activity and give authorities leverage via domain/hosting and user registration requirements; they also impose mandatory censorship obligations on internet-access providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical controls and network-level censorship (Beltelecom gateway, DPI, traffic shaping, blocking lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control over the Internet is centralized with state-owned Beltelecom managing the national gateway; authorities have used deep packet inspection (DPI), traffic shaping and blocking lists to restrict access to websites and throttle or block services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical controls enable large-scale, targeted, or nationwide disruptions (including during protests). The article describes partial internet shutdowns, targeted blocking of dozens of sites, and alleged use of DPI during the 2020 election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyberattacks and DDoS targeting independent media
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported DDoS and other cyberattacks against independent media websites (e.g., BelaPAN, Tut.by) in the run-up to elections or after critical reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cyberattacks function as an informal but effective method to knock critical outlets offline and limit dissemination of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalization and physical repression of journalists covering protests and dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists covering unauthorized demonstrations or working with unregistered media have been arbitrarily detained, arrested, beaten, injured, had equipment seized or destroyed, and in some cases killed under suspicious circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous incidents cited (mass arrests, beatings, forced deletion of media, confiscation of memory cards, detentions during 2020 protests) illustrate physical repression as a censorship tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of media outlets and content as 'extremist' with legal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and prosecutor's offices have declared entire sites, projects or content 'extremist' (e.g., content of Belarusian Investigative Center, Tut.by/Zerkalo.io), enabling bans and criminal penalties for association or distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling as 'extremist' is an administrative/legal shortcut to prohibition, asset freezes and criminal exposure for staff and readers/distributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crackdown on NGOs and journalist associations (revocation of registrations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrations of journalist associations and NGOs (e.g., Belarusian Association of Journalists, Press Club Belarus, PEN Belarus) have been revoked as part of wider attacks on civil society and media pluralism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revocation removes organizational protections and channels for advocacy, further narrowing space for independent journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal prosecution for online edits and social-media content ('discreditation' prosecutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Users and Wikipedia editors have been detained and sentenced for edits and social-media posts accused of 'discrediting' the Republic of Belarus (e.g., Pavel Pernikaŭ sentenced for three Wikipedia edits under article 369-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminalizing routine online contributions chills volunteer editing, online discussion and collaborative knowledge projects; prosecutions extend state control into crowdsourced platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of arts and music via bans, license revocation and economic pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Musicians, bands and films critical of the regime have faced unofficial bans from radio/TV, revocation of concert licenses, cancelled interviews, and economic barriers that create incentives for self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural censorship complements media repression: denial of access to official media and performance venues, licensing controls and economic pressure reduce visibility of dissenting artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of state media narrative to intimidate and delegitimize independent journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: State-run TV and media publish false accusations and invented evidence against journalists and outlets to intimidate audiences and justify repression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufactured narratives serve to discredit independent reporting in the public eye and to rationalize administrative or criminal actions against journalists.
